\abstract{
\textbf{Motivation:} Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome predict the effect of a variant on about a
thousand cell-type-specific tracks. A laboratory studying one cell type must decide which of these predictions to
use. Matching tracks by cell-type name is unreliable, and many cell types are not profiled at all. Laboratories often
measure a few variants before a larger study, but there is no principled way to choose those variants or to turn a
handful of measurements into a choice among a thousand correlated tracks.\\
\textbf{Results:} We present \tp{}. It treats each track as a hypothesis that the assay is an unknown linear
function of the track's predictions, integrates the calibration out in closed form, and starts from the tracks whose
metadata match the cell type. It proposes a pilot panel of variants on which the plausible tracks disagree, and
returns a posterior over tracks and a posterior-weighted prediction for every unmeasured variant. In a pre-registered
test on 125 loci from a saturation mutagenesis reporter assay, eight pilot measurements were non-inferior to the
matched tracks when these existed (mean $+0.010$ in Spearman correlation) and improved on the all-track mean by 0.047
when they were hidden ($P = 3\times10^{-12}$). With eight random measurements, the same inference was worse than not
measuring, and four chosen measurements were as accurate as sixteen random ones. On a second dataset with the cell type hidden, eight pilot measurements beat eight random ones by 0.084.
The conclusions held with model checkpoints that had not been trained on the tested loci, and with a second
foundation model, Enformer, without changing any parameter. The whole panel can be chosen in a single round. In a
third pre-registered test, a reporter assay in induced neurons that no track predicted (matched tracks $\rho=0.07$),
\tp{} did not help and fell 0.01--0.04 below the defaults: it needs a track that carries the assay's signal.\\
\textbf{Availability and implementation:} \tp{} is a Python package and command-line tool (MIT licence) at
\url{https://github.com/ydvislab/AuraGenome-V} \todo{final repository, PyPI name, Zenodo DOI of the submitted version}.
Pre-registrations and all derived results are in the same repository.\\
\textbf{Contact:} \todo{email}\\
\textbf{Supplementary information:} Supplementary data are available at \textit{Bioinformatics} online.}

\keywords{variant effect prediction, genomic foundation models, active model selection, Bayesian experimental design,
massively parallel reporter assays}

\maketitle

%===============================================================================
\section{Introduction}

Deep sequence-to-function models predict the regulatory consequences of non-coding variants from DNA sequence alone
\citep{zhou2015deepsea,avsec2021enformer,linder2025borzoi}. AlphaGenome, the most recent of them, predicts thousands
of genome tracks for hundreds of human cell types and tissues and can score any single-nucleotide variant on all of
them \citep{avsec2026alphagenome}. On saturation mutagenesis benchmarks such as the CAGI5 regulatory challenge
\citep{kircher2019saturation,shigaki2019cagi5} it is among the best available predictors. Its output, however, is not
one prediction per variant but about a thousand, one per track.

A laboratory that studies variants in a particular cell type therefore has to choose which tracks to use. The usual
choice is the tracks whose biosample name matches the cell line. We found this unreliable. Across the 1,018 CAGE,
DNase and ATAC tracks of AlphaGenome, the name-matched track ranked between first and 27th by agreement with measured
effects on our development elements, and the choice changed biological conclusions: at the \textit{PKLR} promoter in
K562 cells, replacing K562 tracks by HepG2 tracks lowered the fraction of significant variants with the correct sign
from 0.96 to 0.69--0.85. Many cell types used in the laboratory, including patient-derived lines, are not profiled,
and then there is no name to match. Adapting the model to a new cell type is possible but requires genome-wide
profiles of that cell type \citep{hingerl2025scooby}.

What a laboratory usually can do is measure a few variants, for example in a pilot reporter assay of 8--16 constructs
before a larger study. This turns the choice of tracks into a label-efficient model selection problem: decide which
variants to measure so that the measurements identify the tracks, or the mixture of tracks, that best predict the
rest \citep{cohn1996active}. Active model selection methods address this for classifiers \citep{karimi2021modelpicker,okanovic2025modelselector,
kay2025coda}. Two features of foundation-model tracks break their assumptions. The tracks are regression outputs on
arbitrary scales, so each must be calibrated to the assay with an unknown slope and offset that a few labels cannot pin
down. And they are a thousand strongly correlated heads of one network, so a few labels often cannot settle which one is best \citep{kuboyama2026labels}, and averaging over
the plausible tracks accounts for this uncertainty \citep{hoeting1999bma}. The problem is
not specific to AlphaGenome: any model with many output heads and a user with a few labels faces it.

Here we present \tp{}, a tool that turns a few measured variants into a decision about which tracks to use.
\tp{} (i) treats each track as a hypothesis with an affine calibration that is integrated out in closed form; (ii)
starts from the metadata-matched tracks and moves away from them only when the measurements contradict them; (iii)
chooses the variants to measure by the classical criterion for discriminating between models
\citep{box1967discrimination}; and (iv) reports a posterior-weighted prediction rather than one selected track. We
evaluated it in pre-registered tests on three mutagenesis reporter datasets, including one where it failed, checked
the dependence on the model's training exposure, and compared it with simpler panels, few-label regression and active model selection methods.

\subsection{Problem}

A regulatory element is studied in cell type $c$. A foundation model gives a predicted effect $x_{t,j}$ for each
candidate variant $j$ on each of $T$ tracks ($T = 1{,}018$ here). The laboratory can measure the effects $y_j$ of $k$
variants, chosen from a pool of variants that can be built, together with the unmutated reference sequence as a
control, so that each effect is measured relative to the reference. We want a prediction $\hat y_j$ for every other variant,
and the panel $S$, $|S| = k$, that makes these predictions as accurate as possible. We measure accuracy by the Spearman
correlation between $\hat y$ and $y$ on variants outside the pool.

\subsection{Tracks as calibrated hypotheses}

Each track's predictions are scaled over the element but not centred, $z_{t,j} = x_{t,j}/\mathrm{sd}_j(x_{t,\cdot})$,
so that the sign keeps the direction of the alternative allele. Hypothesis $t$ states
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
y_j &= a + b\,z_{t,j} + \varepsilon_j,\\
a &\sim N(0,\alpha s^2),\quad b \sim N(0,\beta s^2),\quad \varepsilon_j \sim N(0,(1-\beta)s^2),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $s^2$ is the mean of $y_S^2$. Integrating out $a$ and $b$ gives the marginal likelihood of the measured panel,
\begin{equation}
y_S \mid t \sim N\!\left(0,\ s^2\left[(1-\beta)I + \alpha \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top + \beta z_{t,S} z_{t,S}^\top\right]\right),
\end{equation}
and the posterior $p(t \mid y_S) \propto p(t)\,p(y_S \mid t)$. The predictive mean $m_{t,j} = E[y_j \mid t, y_S]$
follows from the Gaussian conditional, and \tp{} reports the Bayesian model average $\hat y_j = \sum_t p(t\mid y_S)\,
m_{t,j}$ \citep{hoeting1999bma}. The two prior parameters were fixed before any evaluation ($\alpha = 0.1$, $\beta =
0.5$) and never tuned.

\subsection{Metadata prior}

When the model profiles the cell type, the mean of the metadata-matched tracks is a strong default. \tp{} adds it as
one extra hypothesis that holds prior mass $\pi = 0.95$, with a slope prior centred on a positive value, $b \sim
N(\sqrt{\beta}\,s,\ (\beta/4)\,s^2)$, so that a negative slope has prior probability of about 2\%. Single tracks share
the remaining mass. Tracks whose predictions correlate at $r \ge 0.9$ form a family (average linkage, no labels used),
and the prior is split equally between families and then within them, so a family of near-duplicates shares the
prior mass of one track. Without matched tracks there is no default and all mass goes to single tracks. $\pi$ was chosen on the Kircher development
elements and frozen before the Siraj test; unlike the pre-registered tests, the rule for this choice was not committed
before the development runs.

\subsection{Choosing the pilot panel}

The panel is built sequentially from the pool. Given the current posterior, the next variant maximises the
posterior-weighted variance of the hypotheses' predictive means, $\mathrm{Var}_{t \sim p(t\mid y_S)}[m_{t,j}]$, divided
by the expected residual variance. This is the Box--Hill criterion for discriminating between models
\citep{box1967discrimination,rainforth2024modern}. Before any label, all predictive means are zero under the
symmetric slope prior, so the first step uses each track's standardised prediction. Because the choice depends only
weakly on the measured values (Section~\ref{sec:panel}), \tp{} can also return the whole panel before any
measurement, by replacing each chosen variant's label with the current posterior-average prediction.

\subsection{Implementation}

\tp{} is a Python package with a command-line interface \todo{finalise once the package is released; keep in step
with the README}. Its input is a table of predicted effects (variants $\times$ tracks) with track metadata, so it is
not tied to one model; an optional module scores a region with AlphaGenome using the user's own API key (not yet run
from the package with a live key). \texttt{trackpilot suggest} returns a pilot panel of $k$ variants from a pool;
\texttt{trackpilot predict} takes the measured effects and returns the posterior over tracks, predictions for all
variants and a report. For a 1,353-variant element with 1,018 tracks the whole run takes under five seconds on a laptop
(Apple M2 Pro). A reproduction script recomputes with the package every frozen \tp{} result for the first repeat (22
Kircher experiments, 234 numbers; 125 Siraj loci in two cell types, 4,500 numbers) with no difference; the
pre-registered Kircher version (uniform prior) is not covered.

\subsection{Data and predictions}

\textbf{Kircher et al.} \citep{kircher2019saturation} measured every possible substitution in 20 disease-associated
regulatory elements by saturation mutagenesis MPRA. We used the 22 experiments in human cells (27,789 variants).
Five experiments from five regions formed the development set; the other 17 experiments from 11 regions formed the
test set. Several test experiments used cell lines AlphaGenome does not profile, such as SK-MEL-28 and glioblastoma
lines.
\textbf{Siraj et al.} \citep{siraj2026functional,siraj2025data} measured all substitutions in 200-bp oligonucleotides
around fine-mapped trait variants in K562 and HepG2 cells. We used 125 of the 128 published loci (one excluded for a
deletion in the reference, two for having no unique match in GRCh38), 74,975 substitutions each measured in both cell
types. The effect is the log$_2$ fold change of the substituted oligo minus that of the unmutated reference oligo in
the same experiment, which a laboratory measuring a pilot panel would also build.
\textbf{Kosicki et al.} \citep{kosicki2025mpra} measured synthetic transversions at every fourth base of 270-bp tiles
by lentiviral MPRA in WTC11-derived, NGN2-induced excitatory neurons (ENCODE ENCSR548AQS). We used the 328
forward-strand tiles with at least 30 measured substitutions (22,397 measurements), grouped into 159 regions of
overlapping tiles; the effect is the activity of the mutated tile minus that of the reference tile. Neurons are barely
profiled: four AlphaGenome and two Enformer tracks match.
\textbf{Predictions.} We scored every variant by in-silico mutagenesis with AlphaGenome (1-Mb context, default
distilled checkpoint) on all CAGE, DNase and ATAC tracks for human biosamples \citep{avsec2026alphagenome}, which derive
from ENCODE and FANTOM5 \citep{encode2020expanded,fantom2014atlas}. We scored the neuron regions in the same way, and for
Section~\ref{sec:general} the 11 Kircher test regions, 40 randomly drawn Siraj loci and the neuron regions with Enformer \citep{avsec2021enformer} on its 1,322
human CAGE, DNase and ATAC tracks (196-kb context, one forward pass), using the same score: the change in log$_2$ of
the summed signal over a 501-bp window centred on the variant.

\subsection{Evaluation design}
\label{sec:eval}

\textbf{Scenarios.} We hid tracks to simulate three situations: \emph{profiled}, all tracks kept;
\emph{related-only}, the element's own cell line hidden; \emph{unprofiled}, the own and related cell types hidden.
Related cell types were listed from track metadata before any result was seen.
\textbf{Protocol.} In each of 200 repeats, half of an element's variants form the pool that could be measured. Every
method is scored by Spearman correlation on the same variants outside the pool. The unit of analysis is the region
(Kircher; experiments in one region averaged) or the locus (Siraj; two cell types averaged).
\textbf{Pre-registration.} Two pre-registrations were committed with frozen code before the test data were analysed.
For Kircher (version without the metadata prior): H1, the pilot panel beats random panels; H2, it beats the all-track
mean by at least 0.03 with a positive difference in at least 7/11 regions. For Siraj (frozen \tp{}): P1,
non-inferiority to the matched mean in the profiled scenario at $k=8$ (one-sided 95\% bootstrap lower bound above
$-0.02$); P2, at most 15\% of loci worse by more than 0.05; P3, improvement over the all-track mean when unprofiled at
$k=8$ of at least 0.03; P4, improvement over the related-cell mean when related-only at $k=16$. A third, for the neurons (N1--N4: the
analogues of P3, S1, P1--P2 and P4, all at $k=8$), was committed before any variant was scored. Analyses added later
are labelled post hoc.
\textbf{Training data, test sets and homology.} \tp{} trains no model; AlphaGenome is used frozen, and the only labels
are the $k$ measured variants of the element being predicted. No measurement from another element and no evaluation
variant enters the inference. The two test sets (11 Kircher regions, 125 Siraj loci) were fixed before analysis and do
not overlap the development regions. AlphaGenome's training tracks do cover these regions, so we repeated the tests
with, for each locus, the checkpoint whose held-out folds contain every training window overlapping the locus
(\texttt{alphagenome.data.fold\_intervals}). These folds are the Borzoi partitions, which assign genome fragments to
eight folds at random while keeping human and mouse orthologous regions together \citep{linder2025borzoi}. Homologous
sequence within the human genome is not explicitly grouped, so the held-out-fold results reduce, rather than remove,
training exposure. Leave-one-out appears only inside the regression baselines, to
choose a penalty.
\textbf{Baselines.} Label-free: the all-track mean, the matched-track mean and the related-cell mean. Other panels:
random, largest predicted effect, and largest unweighted disagreement. Few-label regression: ridge \citep{hoerl1970ridge} and LASSO
\citep{tibshirani1996lasso} over all tracks; an affine re-fit of the matched mean (\texttt{matched\_cal}); and a
ridge fit on residuals of the calibrated matched mean (\texttt{meta\_ridge}). Active model selection: CODA- and
MODEL SELECTOR-style selection \citep{kay2025coda,okanovic2025modelselector} with our calibrated likelihood. The best
single track chosen with all labels is reported as a reference.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Eight pilot measurements recover a proxy for unprofiled cell types}

With the element's own and related cell types hidden, the label-free alternative is the mean of all tracks.
On the 11 Kircher test regions, eight pilot measurements raised the mean Spearman correlation from 0.296 (all-track
mean) to 0.370, while eight random measurements gave 0.286 (Table~\ref{tab:kircher}, Fig.~\ref{fig:curve}). Both
pre-registered hypotheses held: the pilot panel beat random panels by 0.084 (9/11 regions, $P = 0.0024$) and the
all-track mean by 0.074 (8/11 regions). Gains were largest where the tracks disagreed and the all-track mean was far
from the best track, including \textit{IRF4} in SK-MEL-28, a cell line the model does not profile. They were absent
in elements with very few significant variants (\textit{FOXE1}, 5).

The pre-registered Siraj test confirmed this on 125 new loci (Table~\ref{tab:siraj}, Fig.~\ref{fig:siraj}). Without
matched or related tracks, eight measurements improved on the all-track mean by 0.047 (0.391 to 0.438; $P = 3\times
10^{-12}$; P3). With related-cell tracks only, sixteen measurements improved on their mean by 0.040 (0.412 to 0.452;
$P = 3\times10^{-19}$; P4). Four pilot measurements were as accurate as sixteen random ones (0.402 against 0.404;
Supplementary Table~S7). The gain was concentrated where the default was poor (post hoc): in the quarter of loci where
the all-track mean was furthest from the best track it was 0.133, more than half of that gap, and in the quarter where
it was closest, 0.004 (Supplementary Table~S8).

\subsection{With informative matched tracks, \tp{} is non-inferior to them}

A laboratory working in a profiled cell type would simply use the matched tracks, so the first requirement is not to
do worse than them. On Siraj, with all tracks kept, eight measurements were non-inferior to the matched mean (P1:
$+0.010$, one-sided lower bound $+0.005$ against a margin of $-0.02$), and only 3/125 loci were worse by more than 0.05
(P2: upper bound 6.1\% against 15\%). At $k=16$ the difference was $+0.019$ with one locus harmed. All four
pre-registered hypotheses held. Non-inferiority holds on average, not at every locus: the largest losses were $-0.26$
(one HepG2 locus) and $-0.15$ (one K562 locus).

The metadata prior is what keeps \tp{} level with the matched tracks. Without it, \tp{} was 0.029 below the matched mean on the Kircher test
regions at $k=8$, with 7/11 regions harmed (post hoc): it helped where the matched tracks were poor (\textit{LDLR}:
matched mean 0.24, \tp{} 0.51) but lost where they were good (\textit{SORT1}: 0.65 against 0.48). With the prior, chosen on development
elements before these runs, it was level with the matched mean ($+0.001$, one region harmed; $+0.018$ and none harmed
at $k=16$). The obvious shortcut, re-fitting the matched mean to the same few labels, lowered accuracy on Siraj
($-0.082$ on random panels, $-0.010$ on pilot panels; better at only 1/125 loci with either panel), because the fitted slope is poorly determined and can flip
sign. On the same panel, \tp{} was slightly ahead of \texttt{meta\_ridge} on Siraj ($+0.007$, 97/125 loci) and tied
with it on Kircher.

\subsection{Which variants are measured matters; when they are measured does not}
\label{sec:panel}

Measuring random variants was worse than not measuring: in the unprofiled scenario on Siraj, the same inference
reached 0.342 with random panels, below the label-free all-track mean (0.391), and the pilot panel beat random panels
at 122/125 loci (S1). The specific criterion mattered less (post hoc; Supplementary Table~S4). Choosing variants by
the expected information gain about which track is correct matched the pilot panel (differences $\le 0.003$, also with
a more accurate approximation; Supplementary Table~S6). Panels of the largest predicted effects were as good when matched tracks
were kept, but worse without them (Siraj unprofiled: $-0.028$, 97/125 loci). Most useful in practice, a panel chosen
in one round, before any measurement, was within 0.005 of sequential choice on both datasets, inside our pre-declared
equivalence margin of 0.02. A laboratory can therefore order the whole panel at once. A rule that stops measuring once
the prediction stabilises used about four labels with matched tracks and eight without, but lost 0.013--0.027 against
sixteen labels.

\subsection{Comparison with regression and active model selection}

With the same eight labels, regression over all tracks was much worse than \tp{} (Table~\ref{tab:kircher}), and on
the pilot panel itself \tp{}'s inference still beat LASSO and ridge by 0.023--0.048. Active model selection methods
for classifiers keep a posterior over which candidate is best and report one candidate. We adapted CODA and MODEL
SELECTOR \citep{kay2025coda,okanovic2025modelselector}, gave them our calibrated likelihood, and fixed CODA's prior
weight on development elements (post hoc; Supplementary Table~S5). \tp{} beat the CODA-style selected track by 0.075
on Siraj with matched tracks kept (111/125 loci), by 0.029--0.034 without them, and by 0.051--0.082 on Kircher.
Reporting the baseline's posterior average instead of its single track recovered 0.016--0.026, and with matched
tracks hidden the averaged baseline was level with \tp{}. The advantage therefore comes from two design choices: the
metadata prior when matched tracks exist, and averaging over calibrated tracks instead of selecting one.

\subsection{Robustness}

\textbf{Training exposure.} The default checkpoint was distilled from teachers trained on all training folds, so it has seen tracks over
every tested locus \citep{avsec2026alphagenome}. We repeated both tests with,
for each locus, the AlphaGenome checkpoint that held out its genomic fold, using reading rules committed before the
runs. Absolute accuracies fell by 0.035--0.07, for the matched tracks most (Siraj: 0.474 to 0.402). All four Siraj
hypotheses still held, with larger effects (P1 $+0.024$, P3 $+0.050$, P4 $+0.053$; Supplementary Table~S3). On the 11
Kircher regions the pilot panel's advantage over random panels grew ($+0.093$, 10/11, $P = 0.0015$) and its advantage
over the all-track mean shrank ($+0.054$, $P = 0.062$).
\textbf{Label definition.} Using the published centring of the Siraj effects instead of the reference oligo changed
each pre-registered contrast by at most 0.002 (Supplementary Table~S1).
\textbf{Direction of effects.} On Siraj, the fraction of significant held-out variants with the correct predicted sign
agreed with the rank results (Supplementary Table~S2). On Kircher, the fitted offsets shifted the zero point and
\tp{} called fewer signs correctly than the matched mean ($-0.133$); without the offsets the deficit shrank to $-0.071$
(5 regions better, 4 worse; 95\% interval $-0.21$ to $+0.01$). \tp{} therefore also reports offset-free predictions
for calling directions.
\textbf{Sharing across loci.} A laboratory often studies several loci in one cell type. In a pre-registered extension,
the prior of a new locus mixed the frozen prior with the mean posterior of ten other loci after their own eight-variant
panels (weight 0.75, chosen on 40 development loci). On 85 test loci with the cell type unprofiled, this added 0.012
at eight measurements (65/85 loci, $P = 4\times10^{-8}$), below the pre-registered 0.02, and 0.022 at four; with
matched tracks it stayed non-inferior ($+0.014$, 3/85 loci harmed; Supplementary Table~S9). Sharing helps consistently
but modestly.

\subsection{A second foundation model}
\label{sec:general}

\tp{} uses only the matrix of predictions and the track metadata, so it should carry over to other models. We
re-ran the frozen method, with no parameter changed, on Enformer predictions. The hypotheses and thresholds, the same as
in the AlphaGenome tests, were committed before scoring; Siraj was restricted to 40 randomly drawn loci for compute.
All six hypotheses held (Table~\ref{tab:enformer}). With matched tracks, eight measurements were non-inferior to them
($+0.022$, one-sided lower bound $+0.007$; 1/40 loci worse by more than 0.05). Without them, eight measurements
improved on the all-track mean by 0.052 on Siraj ($P = 4\times10^{-4}$) and by 0.109 on Kircher (8/11 regions), and
beat eight random measurements by 0.097 (10/11 regions, $P = 0.001$). Enformer's tracks were less accurate than
AlphaGenome's (matched mean 0.404 against 0.473 on the same loci), and \tp{}'s gains were at least as
large. Both models' training data cover these regions and include K562 and HepG2, so this test addresses a change of
model, not of cell type.

\subsection{A boundary: an assay that no track predicts}
\label{sec:boundary}

On the two main datasets the cell lines are profiled, so the unprofiled scenarios are simulated. As a cell type that
the models barely profile, we pre-registered the neuron assay and analysed it with both models, changing no parameter.
The main hypotheses did not hold (Table~\ref{tab:enformer}; Supplementary Table~S10). The absolute values show why:
the matched tracks reached a Spearman correlation of only 0.07 with the measured effects, and the all-track mean
0.04--0.05. With eight measurements, \tp{} was 0.02--0.03 below the matched mean, with about 30\% of regions worse by
more than 0.05, and 0.01--0.04 below the all-track mean without matched tracks. The pilot panel still beat random
panels (AlphaGenome $+0.009$, $P = 0.03$; Enformer $+0.005$, $P = 0.17$), but labels with almost no signal that any
track shares move the posterior by noise. The best single track chosen with all labels reached 0.32, yet 0.30 in the
least active quarter of tiles, where substitutions barely change activity (post hoc), so this value mostly reflects
selection among a thousand tracks. When no track carries the assay's signal, a few measurements cannot find one, and
the defaults were the better choice.

%===============================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\tp{} gives laboratories a concrete protocol for using a foundation model in their own cell type: start from the
tracks whose metadata match, measure about eight variants chosen to split the competing tracks, and let the
measurements move the prediction only when they contradict the default. In two pre-registered tests this was
non-inferior to the matched tracks when they existed and recovered 0.04--0.05 in Spearman correlation when they were
missing or only approximate. In a third, on an assay that no track predicted, it did not help, which marks its limit.

Three lessons appear to hold beyond this setting. First, which variants are measured matters as much as how they are
modelled; random measurements made the same inference worse than not measuring. Second, re-fitting a default
predictor to a handful of labels is harmful, and a prior centred on the default avoids this. Third, the output should
be an average: among a thousand correlated heads, the posterior-weighted prediction beat the single most probable
track, and at \textit{HBG1} even the best single track chosen with all labels. These lessons should apply to any model with
many output heads, because \tp{} uses only the matrix of predictions and the track metadata; on Enformer all
pre-registered hypotheses for the two main datasets held without changing a parameter.

\textbf{Limitations.} K562 and HepG2 are profiled by AlphaGenome, so on Siraj the unprofiled scenarios are simulated by
hiding tracks. The one barely profiled cell type we tested in a pre-registered way, induced neurons, came with an
assay that the tracks did not predict, so the case of an unprofiled cell type with a predictable assay rests on a few
Kircher elements. The evaluation is retrospective. Non-inferiority on average does not exclude
losses at single loci (3/125 worse by more than 0.05, the largest $-0.26$). Absolute
correlations are moderate (0.44--0.49 on Siraj), and gains are small where the assay has few significant variants.
\tp{} helps only if at least one track, or a mixture of tracks, is roughly proportional to the assay; on the neuron
assay none was, and \tp{} lost 0.01--0.04 to the defaults.

%===============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

A handful of well-chosen measurements is enough to decide which of a thousand foundation-model tracks to use for a
cell type, as long as some track carries the assay's signal, the decision starts from the metadata default and the measurements
are chosen to discriminate.
\tp{} makes this a two-command step: one to choose the panel and one to turn its measurements into predictions.
